items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.
items.label: Cool Waters
items._genre: experimental / world fusion / folktronica / electronic / African traditional
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是内罗毕新厂牌Cool Waters的首发作品，由德国裔肯尼亚打击乐手Sven Kacirek与Olith Ratengo组成二人组Odd Okoddo，并邀请83岁的肯尼亚东部传统歌手Ogoya Nengo共同录制。Nengo的加入为音乐注入了肯尼亚dodo传统的深厚底蕴，她与Ratengo在地缘和文化上紧密关联，歌词中彼此呼应。Kacirek的Buchla合成器、手打打击乐与套鼓为声音铺设层层电子多节奏纹理，既支撑人声又不掩盖传统根源。以Bara为例，起初廉价的重复击打声与人声形成生硬对比，随后4/4节拍的叮当声、汩汩低音与木琴般的音色逐层浮现，最终融为一体，仿佛一直藏于歌声之下。Sarah则展示了更激烈的质感，电子失真在Ratengo人声高潮处悄然介入。整张专辑体现了不同文化间真诚的对话，根源变为前卫，创新如千年古调。

items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.
items.label: Songs of Compassion
items._cn_summary: Dorothy Moskowitz 与 Francesco Paolo Paladino、Luca Chino Ferrari 合作的《Songs of Compassion》收录十一首歌曲，融合前卫作曲手法与非西方调性逻辑。钢琴作为主体音色在不同声层间穿插游走，搭配弦乐、木管、合成器铺底与金属质感声响，整体呈现非线性的空间感。歌词层面延续1960年代抗议歌曲传统，《Pale Wanderer》直指威权主义的共谋结构，《Charlottesville》以已故 Joe Byrd 合写的诗作回应当代极右运动。Moskowitz 的演唱不依附常规旋律走向，而是以意识流方式服务每个词语的语义重量。钢琴演奏本身亦构成独立声部，承担类似希腊合唱的评述功能。这是一张将音乐实验与社会批判结合的作品，对习惯西方式和声听觉习惯的听众构成认知挑战与拓展。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items._cn_summary: Tako Toki 乐队的第二张专辑以自制的奇异乐器为核心卖点——他们用废料和杂物亲手打造了包括 tassofons、kitchenofon 等一系列原创乐器，并在现代录音技术下呈现出令人惊讶的准确音准与丰富质感。专辑横跨多种文化音乐风格：klezmer 风格的欢笑单簧管与巴松管对话、cumbia 风格的西班牙语合唱与拉丁打击乐、afrobeat 风的木鱼与沙锤交织、samba 节奏的悠扬长笛，以及带有中东迷幻色彩的旋律线。演奏中大量即兴段落展现了扎实的演奏功底，旋律乐器时常以爵士化的切分节奏游离于节拍之外。专辑以轻松幽默的方式庆祝人类对节奏与旋律的普遍热爱，同时提醒听众：音乐的本质不在于乐器的材质，而在于人们总能设法创造声音的本能。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._genre: experimental jazz / folk fusion / improvisation / electronic
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是挪威Camilla Hole Trio继融合科幻合成器与传统音乐的前作之后的最新作品，主奏乐器为高音萨克斯，融合挪威西部民谣旋律与爵士即兴。三人组的角色分配刻意模糊，开篇曲目以挪威传统Springleik舞曲旋律为骨架，Hole先用萨克斯陈述旋律，Kalman以低音提琴和模块合成器、Nesheim以鼓和颤音琴提供节奏支撑与色彩，随后旋律在乐器之间流转，乐曲逐步走向自由的即兴展开。低音提琴与萨克斯的齐奏、颤音琴对节奏的拓展，使传统旋律在保持骨架的同时获得了开放的结构。整张专辑延续了探索本国民谣之外的音乐语汇这一脉络，将北欧民间素材置于爵士与电子的交汇点上进行处理。

items.body: From solo piano to orchestra, the music in this genre bears witness to life’s atrocities; it reflects the change of seasons; it seeks to console and uplift. Our top pick reintroduces us to a fallen friend, but new composers make an impact as well; one can never tell where the next great album will come from. Soon the leaves will begin to fall again, and then the snow, and then the rain, and then it will be summer. These composers bring us through life’s transitions, always looking forward to the next, teaching us the wisdom of cycles through the beauty of notes. Our cover image is taken from Jean-Michel Blais‘ mirador, covered below. Jóhann Jóhannsson has been gone nearly a decade now, and his absence is still felt. After a trickle of posthumous releases, we had grown resigned to the thought that we might never again hear new music from the composer. Meanwhile, Adam Wiltzie was working on unfinished pieces from a collaboration begun before the composer’s untimely death. We can think of no one better to tackle such a project. Adding to the sadness is the knowledge that Steve Albini helped with the production before he too was lost to the sands of time. Friendship Survival Guide is a tribute and a sonic keepsake; it’s a minor miracle that it exists at all. The first video is the beginning of a narrative thread; we can’t wait to see the rest! (Deutsche Grammophon, September 18). Also on Deutsche Grammophon, Icelandic composer Hildur Guðnadóttir reimagines her back catalogue with Robert Ames and the DSO Berlin. This Will Be Us breathes new life into these pieces and is preceded by non-album track “Floods” (October 23). The cover of Jean-Michel Blais‘ mirador looks like Max from Where the Wild Things Are sleeping off his evening; but it may also be a young man dreaming of adventure. The album is an ode to childhood imagination, bolstered by copious choirs and swirling strings (Arts & Crafts, September 25). Third Coast Percussion returns with Vernacular, the percussion ensemble’s 25th album. Jlin is now a full performing member, as heard on the opening single Premonition (Rockwell, October 23). Klara Lewis‘ Opening is already out, one of autumn’s early highlights. The album is awash in shades of blue, from art to music. After the abraded loops of “Ta Min Hand “, the set moves from form to abstraction, shifting like light through falling leaves (Editions Mego, September 4).   Justyna Jablonska‘s Unforeseen is a diverse set that addresses migration and memory through song, spoken word, voice and field recordings. The artist’s cello shines throughout the set, which culminates in a surprising rendition of “Shchedryk,” known to modern listeners as “Carol of the Bells” (Alumni Records Glasgow, September 4). Earlier this year, cellist Gaspar Claus impressed us with the score to French film Un Monde Violent. Now he returns with CELLS, which includes a contribution from Matt Elliott (Third Eye Foundation). The album is released September 25 on InFiné. Inspired by the work of visual artist James Turrell, Alyssa Weinberg‘s Pieces of Light, performed by cellist Gabriel Cabezas, plays with permutations of illumination. The album is preceded by the single ultraviolet (MASS MoCA, October 2).   Clerestory reflects its title, which refers to the windows in the upper section of walls, as found in churches. Jules Reidy uses this image to color the music, which highlights the interplay between shadow and light and whose single-track Side A is brought to light by JACK Quartet (Thrill Jockey, September 25). Twin Cities four-piece The Dust of Suns Ensemble offers Alyosha is a series of miniatures, inspired by Dostoyevsky, but with a playful aura. Released on September 1, early copies of the album are available on precious 10″ vinyl. We don’t receive many hurdy-gurdy albums, much less albums of hurdy-gurdy with violin and cello. Almost Starlight is one of these, recorded in a medieval church by Jem Finer (yes, that Jem Finer, from The Pogues!), John Matthias and Jay Auborn. The results are magical, mystical and ceremonial (Touch, September 4). Simon Goff‘s electronic chamber music is packed with violin and viola, with guest appearances by Anne Müller on cello. Interior Realms – vol. 1 is upbeat and life-affirming, on the surface a study of architecture but beneath this a treatise on the soul (Sonic Pieces, September 10). We can never tell where more eaze will head next, which is part of her appeal. On valley and structure, she heads for the heart of modern composition, even offering a score booklet. A host of guest starts decorates the set with new timbres and additional grace (Thrill Jockey, October 9).   Goldmund‘s In Each Moment is a gorgeous fall collection, inspired by the teachings of Buddhist nun Sister Dang Nghiem. The piano notes are as delicate as incense wafting to the sky, enhanced by some gentle ambient textures, producing a sense of perfect peace (Nettwerk, October 9). Chad Lawson‘s lowercase hush is as serene as can be, a prelude to winter. On held by evening, one can hear the almost hear the leaves as they start to fall (Decca, September 11). Jumping straight into that faraway season, Volodja Brodsky‘s piano-based Winterglare recalls the sun’s low angle in Estonia’s winter (We Are Busy Bodies, October 2). Piano player meets machine on The End is a Beginning, from the aptly named Postmodern Machine. The beats are warm and plentiful, but the ivories still hold court (Moderna, September 11). Some may recall that Björk’s first film role was in the feminist retelling of the Grimm tale The Juniper Tree. Forty years after it was written by Nietzchka Keene, the film receives a new score from Midori Hirano. The artist manages to tap into the tenderness and leans into the unsettling tension, with piano as the anchor and synthesizer as the encroachment (Viernulvier/Thrill Jockey, October 2). Ingfrid Breie Nyhus‘ Silkegul – Slåttepiano III is the third in a series of albums that investigate Norwegian folk traditions by means of the piano. As the nights grow longer, the notes will seem more and more fitting, like tales told around a fire (Lab, October 9).   Billed as a classical soul pianist, Alexis Ffrench releases the lush 24, two dozen pieces meant to comprise the soundtrack of a day. With tracks such as In Flight, crossover success is virtually guaranteed (Sony Classical, October 2). Pianist Sofi Paez releases Bodies of Water, inspired by Iceland’s diversity of natural beauty. Ocean is the first single (OPIA Community, September 25). Doubts and Loves Like a Mole is the new EP from pianist Nathan Schubert, preceded by the peaceful, brass-inflected single Schillerpromenade (Bigo & Twigeitti, October 2). Brandon Hopkins follows Three Commutes with Piano Etudes, Book I, six works of tender wisdom (September 25). On the cover of conditions for observing light, pianist Cephas Azariah seems to have been shot through with a sunbeam. The metaphor applies to the composer’s work, which also touches on ambient and electronic territory, while searching fro radiance in all of its forms (Anjunachill, September 3). With radiant contributions from Clarice Jensen and Spencer Zahn, Sova (Sophia Vastek) can do no wrong. As one might expect from the title, early single “Heavy Shit” is an exercise in darkness, but the album Alight! is a study of contrasts, anchored by Sova’s exquisite keys (Hout, September 4). Double bass and electronics merge on Fragments, an album long in the making; Fragment I debuted in 2025. By blending genres, ZKHR hopes to appeal to multiple audiences (September 19).   Dobrinka Tabakova has been accumulating the pieces of Stone Trail for nearly a quarter-century; now they are gathered in one place. The album is graced with numerous collaborators, and is one of our furthest-out releases, dropping November 13 on NMC. The first half of Episodic Memory includes a murder ballad, but the second is a vibrant instrumental suite that comments on the experience of trauma. Exceptet and Bendon Randall-Myers handle both with aplomb (cmntx, October 9). Daniella Ljungsberg splits Other Plans between vocal and instrumental pieces, but when she sings, she does so with reverence, honoring the Baroque nature of these tender Nordic folk tales (ORTHODOX, October 2). Alfredo Ovalles and Black Page Orchestra present The Art of Parties on September 18, preceded by the inviting single Dance! (PARMA). Richard Allen

items.body: Review by yarstruly — Clicking 5 but really 4.5, 4 is too low!Simultaneously posted to my blog (Scott's Song by Song Spotlights), with additional links and information.PsychoYogi are a UK prog band formed in 2010 and led by guitarist/vocalist/composer Chris Ramsing. The line up has evolved since their 2011 debut but has stabilized over the last few releases. Chris recently reached out to me to review the band's latest album "A World of Danger", released on November 28, 2025. As with my previous review, while it is not brand new or pre-release, it is certainly not an "old" album. This is their tenth studio album. According to Chris: "There is no theme, the main thing that connects the tunes is the downfall of mankind in the 21st century, each song has its own story?"As always, I receive no additional compensation other than the review copy of the album, and I always call it like I hear it. This is a cold listen.The line up for the album is:- Chris Ramsing / guitar, vocal- Izzy Stylish / bass- Tim Smart / trombone- Ben Woodbine-Craft / violin- Justin Casey / drums(How many prog bands sport a full-time trombonist? I would suspect there are few others, if any!)Track 1 - World of Danger (5:55)Jumping right in with the title track. It begins with a cool jazzy rhythm, and Tim Smart's trombone is prominent from the get-go. This has a very cool groove. The vocals could come out a little more but still sounds good. Chris has a reverse-recorded guitar solo at around the 2-minute mark. Loving the vibe of this. The arrangement is very creative. Izzy and Justin are a very talented rhythm section. The feeling is slightly sinister, like a film noir gangster. This really lives up to its title and sets the stage for a world of danger. Track 2 - Sometimes (2:49)This stays jazzy, but with a different groove. Lots of timing changes. I like Justin's cymbal work; not to mention the guiro and other assorted percussion novelties. The overall effect is slightly disorienting and implies a bit of a break with sanity. The closing verse kind of sums it up: In the asylum we're safe for a while and there's no expectations of who we should be, time doesn't matter and words have no meaning and less information is key.Another very cool track, albeit a short one!Track 3 - Blue in Rap City (3:05)The title is certainly a play on George Greshwin's "Rhapsody in Blue". The jazzy vibes continue, this time in a "joyfully strutting down the street" kind of way. This is such a unique sounding band! This one has a bit of a swing to it, but some odd meters keep you guessing. Izzy is walking all over the bass! Chris plays some classic jazz solos along the way. Tim Smart's trombone is very prominent. Ben Woodbine-Craft's violin, thus far, hasn't stood out, but has contributed in an ensemble serving fashion. Another fun, unique track!Track 4 - Mutual Agenda (2:59)The bass and drums play a few short rhythmic phrases, then, right on cue, the band kicks in and Ben is featured on violin. I promise this is a cold listen, typed in real time as I play each track. The contrasts between the instrumental segments are very interesting. The instrumental phrases are like a big band jazz thing, but the verses have vocals with guitar with a chorus effect on it. Another track that is unlike anything I have ever heard! (That's a good thing.)Track 5 - The Strangest Places (3:01)An air of mystery and Eastern flavor surrounds this one. Again, I'd like the vocals to be more out front. This feels like a snake-charmer dance. Super-cool! These guys are very talented! I like it! Just wish it were longer!Track 6 - Do That Dance (2:26)As we might expect, the jazziness continues. This one is a bit "sultry". The lyrics deal with individualism, and not falling in line with the crowd:I don't want to do that dance, smoke that thing or wear those pants, Parties make me feel remote, help me find the antidote.I don't want to pierce my nose, shave my head or decompose, fake a smile to win romance, I don't want to do that dance.A quick, fun little track.Track 7 - Moron (2:56)This has a tom-tom, smoky night club from back in the day, kind of a vibe. Very quirky! Middle Eastern style melodies help flavor the sound. Another cool, but short, jazzy track.Track 8 - For the Future (4:30)Belly-dance vibes abound! Very syncopated rhythms and odd meters are a big part of this. I like the unison instrumental phrases that are as tight as can be. This one makes me bob my head as I'm listening and typing. I like the vocal layering in the closing vocal section. The instruments take over to close it out. Cool tune!Track 9 - In Sight of the Goal (4:15)This one is also very syncopated, but not as bouncy as its predecessor. Much of it is in a meter of 7. Their arrangements are all so uniquely "them". Good track, but maybe not the strongest track on the album.Track 10 - Wonder Why (3:52)This one is a little bluesy; yet proggy too. Chris has such a nice, clean guitar tone. The trombone is what really gives the band their flavor. The final verse really asks a profound question:There's something troubling me, I can't begin to see,why children starve to please the rich,I'm sure you all agree and what will be will be.Kind of the state of the world right now.OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:This album goes to show that progressive isn't always defined by long tracks and head-spinning technically difficult phrases. That should not imply that this isn't a very talented band; they indeed are quite talented. This was a very difficult album for me, not in the sense of not liking it?I liked it a lot?but rather in the sense of having references jump into my mind for points of comparison. While I was aware of PsychoYogi prior to hearing this album, I hadn't heard very much until now. That is a situation that I intend to rectify, as I have added every available album to my streaming library. They don't sound like anyone that I am familiar with. And that is no easy task with there being so much music out there to listen to under the prog umbrella. Overall, I give this a 4.5 out of 5 (90%). If you already know PsychoYogi, then you already know it's unique. If, like me before listening to this album, you don't know them, I would highly recommend checking them out. If their earlier albums are anything like this one, they have carved out a unique niche in our prog world.
items._cn_summary: PSYCHOYOGI 的《World of Danger》是一张以爵士律动为骨架的前卫摇滚专辑，吉他、长号、小提琴与贝斯鼓组构成独特的乐器配置，融合了爵士摇摆感与前卫摇滚的复杂节奏变化。Chris Ramsing 的作曲贯穿影片般的叙事氛围，从黑帮式的阴郁律动到精神病院般的失序感，每首曲目独立成篇，共同映射21世纪人类文明的衰落主题。长号的突出地位、贝斯的活跃walking line、以及小提琴的合奏点缀，形成了罕见的前卫爵士摇滚混合声响。专辑不依赖流行化结构，注重氛围营造与器乐互动，是独立厂牌下对前卫爵士融合路线的一次扎实实践，适合追求复杂节奏与即兴质感的听众。

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — A Dark Poem, Part III: The Messiah Complex by Green Carnation is a nice ending to the trilogy of albums they've released since last year, but compared to the first 2, it isn't as gripping or spectacular. With only 3 songs, along with a long orchestral suite that almost acts like the trilogy's end credits, the songs just aren't as strong compared to the outstanding material on the first 2 parts. But besides that, the overall musicianship is outstanding, with great mixes of gothic, progressive, folk and doom metal, and vocalist Kjetil Nordhus giving an impressive diverse performance, proving again that he's one of metal's most underlooked gems. I'd give this a high 6 to low 7 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is The Messiah Complex.
items._genre: experimental metal / progressive / gothic metal / doom metal / folk metal
items._cn_summary: Green Carnation 三年三部曲的终章，以三首歌曲加一段长篇管弦乐组曲构成终曲式收束。评论者认为其整体器乐水准出色，将哥特、前卫、民间与厄运金属元素融合，主唱 Kjetil Nordhus 展现出多样化的演唱能力，被认为是金属界被低估的歌手之一。然而相比前两部分，本作的歌曲强度有所下滑，抓人程度与精彩度不及前作。评论者给出 6 到 7 分的区间评分，推荐曲目为同名曲 The Messiah Complex。整体而言，这是一张融合多种金属子风格的实验性作品，但作为系列终章在曲目深度上略显不足。

items.body: Review by alainPP — A 13th EP, serving as a prelude to the full CD release later this year. It features diverse influences?progressive rock, classical, and electronic?with echoes of Pink Floyd, Marillion, Steven Wilson, and other British acts."Smile, Smile, Smile," which will appear on the upcoming CD, offers a technical, electro-crossover sound; musically, it flirts with the work of Steven Wilson and Brian Eno, while the lyrics draw inspiration from Philip K. Dick. The sound is designed to reflect the protagonist's disorientation, creating an atmosphere that is latent, schizoid, and oppressive."The Amber Hour"?the first of two instrumental tracks?is gentle, atmospheric, and jazzy, featuring shimmering guitar work. Its sound leans toward Gilmour-esque and Floydian territory, characterized by melting guitar tones and enveloping synths."Broken Arrow" is more experimental and eclectic, driven by wild, seemingly untamable synths. It features a frenetic pace and a swirling melody reminiscent of the 80s and 90s?the previous millennium?while also offering a fresh, punchy pop-crossover vibe.
items._cn_summary: 这是英国乐队Hats Off Gentlemen It's Adequate的第13张EP，作为全长专辑的前奏发行。三首作品分别探索了不同方向：主打曲融合电子与前卫摇滚元素，编曲技术性强，歌词灵感来源于菲利普·K·迪克，氛围营造出迷失与压迫感；器乐曲《The Amber Hour》以吉他与合成器为主，气质接近Gilmour式的梦幻处理，带有爵士即兴色彩；《Broken Arrow》则走向更激进的实验领域，合成器失控般地铺陈，节奏密集，旋律在八十至九十年代复古合成器流行与新鲜跨界流行之间游走。整体来看，这张EP在传统前卫摇滚框架内注入了相当程度的电子实验性与音色探索，融合意图明确。

items.body: This album is a collaboration between the American Black-Metal and Experimental projects Sutekh Hexen (whom we already know well) and Hissing. The release comprises two lengthy tracks, originally performed live by the two bands—one in 2017 and the other in 2019. These recordings have now been reworked and refined to create “SH:HS”. What you hear seems to be primarily the result of meticulous improvisation, shaped into a form that incorporates a wide range of influences. It starts out as Dark-Ambient, quickly evolves into pure Drone, and then transforms into a truly Cinematic passage that, in turn, shifts into something considerably noisier. Growling vocals also emerge, adding to the overall sense of darkness. The second track stands out for its boundless sound manipulation and myriad effects, eventually losing itself in a relentless—and, to my ears, somewhat grating—Hardcore rhythm. “SH:HS” sounds like a musical crossroads where various genres seek an outlet, ultimately merging into a dark, cohesive whole. For me, however, it is the first track that really sticks with me. (Rating:6½). Listen to “LAX”: LAX by Sutekh Hexen & Hissing About Sutekh Hexen and Hissing Sutekh Hexen is an American experimental black metal project based in Oakland, California, originally formed in San Francisco. The band has been active for over a decade, dating back to at least 2010, and started out anonymously with three limited demo tapes that combined atmospheric black metal with noise electronics and dark ambient. Over the years its recording and live line-up has drawn on a wide cast of musicians, including A.C. Way, Demian Johnston, Joshua Churchill, Kevin Yuen, Lee Camfield, Mackenzie Chami, Ryan Jencks, Samuel Torres and Scott Miller. Sutekh Hexen’s release chronology includes the self-titled album “Sutekh Hexen” (2019, Cyclic Law), the collaborative album “P:R:I:S:M” with Funerary Call (2023, Cyclic Law/Sentient Ruin), and “Primeval” (2025, Cyclic Law/Breath Sun Bone Blood), an album built entirely from acoustic strings, percussion and wind instrumentation. Hissing is a death/black metal band from Seattle, Washington, whose members include Joe O’Malley, Sam Pickel and Zach Wise. Its discography includes the albums “Permanent Destitution” (2018) and “Hypervirulence Architecture” (2022). Sutekh Hexen and Hissing first shared a release with a split album on Flenser Records in 2017, the same year one of the two live performances reworked for “SH:HS” took place. The second performance dates from 2019. Both recordings have now been refined into the two tracks that make up “SH:HS”, released digitally and on CD via Cyclic Law.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由美国实验黑金属乐队 Sutekh Hexen 与西雅图死亡/黑金属乐队 Hissing 合作完成，将 2017 与 2019 年两场现场演出重新混音加工后呈现为两首长篇作品。音乐从黑暗氛围出发，滑入持续音色的低鸣，随后展开接近电影配乐的画面感段落，再转入密集噪音与咆哮人声。第二首着重于极端的声音操控与效果叠加，最终陷入生硬的硬核节奏律动。整体而言，这是一次高度即兴化的跨类型实验，将黑暗氛围、持续音、黑金属、噪音与硬核节拍熔铸为一个阴暗的整体。第一首的层次递进与氛围张力最为突出，第二首虽在声响实验上大胆，但部分段落稍显刺耳。小厂牌 Cyclic Law 的发行保持了地下的独立性。

items.body: Between the teeth of misery The hunger takes a hold of me I take my time now I make it right now ACTORS have always sounded like they knew that the nightclub was going to get closed down by gentrification eventually, which may explain why their new album Our Love Will Live Forever hits with such peculiar force: this time the closing hour has stopped being metaphor, and now indeed is the time to party like there is no tomorrow, because tomorrow is never guaranteed. Mastermind Jason Corbett suffered a serious cardiac emergency while making the record, and suddenly all those polished guitars, black-glass synthesizers, romantic fixations, and doomed little dances had to answer to the wails of an ambulance. “Getting wheeled into an emergency room and spending days in the cardiac care unit put me in a state of deep reflection,” Corbett reflects. “Would I finish the album? Would I ever be on a stage again? I was given a second chance to cherish every experience and live in the moment. My goal was to bring that energy to the album.” You can hear it. These songs carry the nervous velocity of somebody who has seen the trapdoor beneath ordinary life and decided to dance directly over it. The title predates Corbett’s hospitalization. Our Love Will Live Forever is engraved on his grandparents’ tombstone, which already carried enough emotional freight before Death suddenly walked into the studio and pulled up a chair. Afterward, the words became a dare…if everybody knows this grim appointment is coming, then what are you doing with the hours beforehand? Left On Read is a beautifully petty modern nightmare, romance reduced to glowing glass, silence, and the humiliating authority of an unanswered message. Corbett turns digital abandonment into old-fashioned psychic damage while the band dresses the anxiety in immaculate synths and guitars. Once upon a time heartbreak required somebody to slam a door. Now your phone can ruin an entire evening without making a sound. Then CTRL starts issuing orders. Its hook has the merciless efficiency of advertising copy, the rhythm grabs the hips before permission has been granted, and guitar lines cut across the synths with sudden flashes of attitude. Depeche Mode’s leather poise, the Human League’s pop nerve, Bootblacks, and the exploratory rush of early Simple Minds can all be detected in the bloodline, but ACTORS have been doing this too long to sound like record collectors arranging their shelves. “(CTRL) is a rally cry, a reaction to a world spinning out of control,” says Corbett. “Being true to yourself is an act of resistance.” That sentence could have come off a placard. On the record, it becomes physical. Elsewhere, memory, desire, fear, and attachment keep colliding without turning the album into some tasteful meditation on mortality suitable for soft lighting and solemn nodding. Corbett’s production at Jacknife Sound stays beautifully controlled while allowing plenty of abrasion around the edges. Drums land with authority, basslines keep the blood moving, guitars carve openings through the synths, and his voice maintains that familiar balance between romantic composure and somebody quietly coming apart behind it. By album three, ACTORS have nothing left to prove about belonging to post-punk. Our Love Will Live Forever is after a nastier question: what happens when mortality quits being philosophy and becomes paperwork, hospital lights, machines, and the possibility that your unfinished record stays unfinished? Their answer makes excellent sense. Turn it up while you still can. Our Love Will Live Forever is out now via Artoffact Records, on vinyl, CD, and all major digital and streaming platforms. Listen to the album below and order it here. Our Love Will Live Forever by ACTORS ACTORS go on tour throughout Europe and Canada this autumn! The tour takes ACTORS across Europe in September, with stops in Germany, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Spain, France, and the UK before heading back to Canada in October. The run includes festival appearances, club shows, and a closing stretch through Vancouver, Edmonton, and Calgary. items.body: I will be there in a vintage Mugler negligee come and go, take your troubles away… Viva l’amore! Long live love, without pain. Everybody knows the bargain is impossible, which makes singing it feel deliciously reckless. What began as words for one lover has widened into a hymn for appetite, where pleasure becomes moral, beauty practically compulsory. Sweet Love Under Tyranny has a name that sounds ready to be painted across the side of a limousine headed for a disco or a minor apocalypse, and Viva L’Amore, the second track from the project’s forthcoming self-titled EP, carries itself with the same expensive nerve. The Los Angeles producer and vocalist takes darkwave, gothic pop, and the synthetic romance of Italo disco, then stuffs them into a song concerned with the oldest bad idea in civilization: that love might be separated from pain. The song lives on movement. A Synclavier bass strum enters the hook with enough physical authority to make stillness seem impolite, while Matia Simovich’s co-production keeps the arrangement spacious enough for every drum hit, synth accent, and vocal turn to register. Lilian Void’s solo adds a flash of virtuosity without turning the record into a showroom, and Josh Bonati’s mastering preserves the dynamics rather than crushing everything into one gleaming rectangle. There is luxury everywhere, although the luxury has teeth. This quality suits the lyric, which imagines midnight desire as temporary exile from consequence: champagne, sea air, vintage Mugler, secret rooms outside ordinary time. Sweet Love Under Tyranny explains its origin with equal appetite: “It’s about a quickening all of the truly good and beautiful things in life: love, food, sex… silk chiffon… the end of summer just before fall… the real reasons for living! The hook wafted into my consciousness after a family trip to Sicily when the salt was still fresh on my skin from the sea, and I was full of wine, and pasta, and life from the spirit of the place. Initially it was just “Viva l’amore” repeated on the hook, but my friend Mayumi suggested I alternate with senza dolore, which of course, was precisely the move.” Listen to Viva L’Amore and pre-order the Sweet Love Under Tyranny EP here. Sweet Love Under Tyranny EP by Sweet Love Under Tyranny Viva L’Amore also sharpens the promise of Sweet Love Under Tyranny’s self-titled EP, due November 6 via à La Carte Records on digital formats and, for the first time, vinyl. Clear and two-tone black-in-clear editions suit music this obsessed with surfaces, sensation, and presentation. Beneath all that elegance sits a blunt proposition: life is brief, the bottle is open, desire is present, and somebody had better dance. items.body: Where’s the joy in this all? Where’s the light in the dark My hands hide my tears, I feel so lost This first day of Fall Summer does not end so much as loosen its grip. The green world, having spent itself extravagantly, begins to remember that fullness and disappearance are partners. Leaves turn because life is not obliged to remain at its brightest. The air cools, light lowers, and what seemed permanent reveals itself as a passing arrangement. Autumn teaches without speaking: beauty depends upon change, and change upon loss. Yet nothing is truly lost; forms simply withdraw into other forms. The falling leaf is not a failure of the tree, but part of its rhythm. So too, perhaps, are we, within nature’s larger turning. Despair can still dance. Since forming in Los Angeles in 2021, DECEITS (Kevin Moreno and Francisco Saenz) have dragged the music back toward blood, romance, and movement, pulling from the Spanish-language records that surrounded them growing up and letting those rhythms rub against basslines built for dark rooms. The First Day Of Fall comes from a worse place. Moreno wrote it the day before his birthday, during a morning when the approaching occasion felt less like celebration than accusation. Birthdays carry the ridiculous expectation that happiness should report for duty on schedule, and the song turns that pressure inside out. Here is somebody staring at another year of existence and wondering whether disappearance might be easier. When Moreno sings, “I dream to be forgot,” the line lands with the ugly simplicity of a thought you wish you had never admitted to yourself. The music, meanwhile, moves with enough force to keep despair from becoming static. Bass sits at the center with a cold, muscular authority, pushing against a hard drum pattern while guitars spread reverb across the track in broad, abrasive sheets. Gothic synthesizers hang behind the rhythm section, giving the song a sense of scale without smothering its punk impulse. There is a useful contradiction in hearing music this alive carrying words preoccupied with erasure, as though the body has decided to keep moving even while the mind is filing objections. Moreno’s voice makes that conflict sharper. In the quieter passages he bends into a soft, almost romantic delivery, letting the words hover close to the ear before climbing toward a piercing upper register when the arrangement surges. The shift feels less theatrical than involuntary, like restraint finally losing the argument. The production owes an obvious debt to the cavernous records of the 1980s gothic underground, though the mix has enough present-day weight to keep the references from turning archival. Reverb creates depth around the guitars and vocals, but the bass and drums remain immediate, physical, and slightly dangerous. Every element seems placed to preserve tension rather than polish it away. Listen to The First Day of Fall below: The First Day of Fall turns a private crisis into forward motion, carrying self-erasure, birthday dread, and the changing season inside a rhythm section that keeps pressing ahead. With the Hurt As Much As Me Tour 2026 on the horizon, DECEITS sound ready to take that contradiction straight into the room, where pain becomes volume and motion becomes temporary proof of life. Maybe that is DECEITS’ gift: making anguish feel communal without sanding down its teeth. Listen to The First Day of Fall below and order the single here. items.album: Berlin Post-Punk Veterans Golden Apes Confront the Half-Damaged Self in Video for “Resistance”
items.excerpt: Every definition closes off certain possibilities. Naming an experience can help us understand it, but a name can also become a verdict, reducing a person to one fixed account of who they are and what their wounds mean. Human beings are rarely so easy to settle. We contradict ourselves, bear the consequences of our choices, and continue to change even after others believe they understand us. Resistance may begin there: in defending the right to remain complex, unresolved, and unfinished. Berlin
items.body: Every definition closes off certain possibilities. Naming an experience can help us understand it, but a name can also become a verdict, reducing a person to one fixed account of who they are and what their wounds mean. Human beings are rarely so easy to settle. We contradict ourselves, bear the consequences of our choices, and continue to change even after others believe they understand us. Resistance may begin there: in defending the right to remain complex, unresolved, and unfinished. Berlin post-punk and darkwave mainstays Golden Apes enter that unsettled territory with Resistance, the first single from The Sun Came Up Tremendously, their twelfth studio album, due September 18 through Icy Cold Records. Released today alongside a film written and directed by vocalist Peer Lebrecht, the song treats opposition as an internal friction: the force that keeps identity from hardening into a final shape, even when certainty would be easier. Resistance opens on a resonant guitar figure, answered by a single low keyboard tone. Hi-hats enter with a dry sizzle; Christian Lebrecht’s bass gives the piece forward pressure, while wavering synths and Salomon Bosse’s drums steadily enlarge the frame. Once the heavier guitar figure lands, the track assumes the emotional scale of mid-’80s gothic rock. Peer Lebrecht sings in a deep baritone that stays composed as the arrangement grows dense, and the guitars follow the cadence of his lines with a spring-loaded post-punk lift before thickening between verses. At intervals, the drums loosen into splashes, and the rhythm pulls back, leaving more air around Peer’s euphoric delivery. A clean, melodic guitar solo settles at the center point, almost plain in its design; its calm gives the vocal’s return greater weight. The measured bass, sober guitar tone, and baritone gravity recall Scottish cult band Lowlife, while the surrounding textures remain recognizably Golden Apes. The band describes the song’s central idea in terms of identity, complexity, and damage: “…Maybe that is the actual resistance. Not resistance against an external system, but resistance against final form. Against definition. Against the temptation to trade complexity for peace. Half-damaged instead of neatly resolved. I am the enemy…” Lebrecht’s film, based on a lucid dream by Vito Schneider, transfers that internal struggle to an abandoned clinical ward rendered in sickly greens and exhausted amber. A striped spinning top travels down an empty corridor; barefoot figures in hospital gowns occupy tiled rooms and enact private systems whose purpose never fully declares itself. One scrubs water from a floor into a bucket, another fills a bathtub, one drinks from a metal cup, and another holds an open umbrella beneath a dry ceiling. A solitary player moves grapes across a checkerboard, while a black telephone waits inside a star-lined suitcase. Elsewhere, a reel-to-reel machine runs beside clasped hands, as though recording testimony from a room that has forgotten its questions. Golden Apes perform throughout the ward, each member stationed apart in bathrooms, bare rooms, and passages. High overhead angles flatten bodies into diagrams, while the repetition of circular objects—the spinning top, fruit, reel hubs, and drum heads—turns the building into a machine for processing unresolved thought. In the closing coda, a black-clad figure carries armfuls of hospital gowns into a laundromat and feeds them into a washer. The garments pass through one more cycle, suggesting cleansing, erasure, recurrence, or all three at once. Watch the video for Resistance below: For more than two decades, Golden Apes have moved among post-punk, darkwave, gothic rock, indie rock, and electronic experiment, bringing delicate guitar melodies, driving bass, and Peer Lebrecht’s sonorous voice into a language of their own. The Berlin group has appeared at Wave-Gotik-Treffen, Castle Party, and Murder of Crows, toured across Europe, the United States, Canada, and Russia, and shared stages with And Also The Trees, The Chameleons, Pink Turns Blue, Clan of Xymox, She Past Away, Whispering Sons, TRAITRS, Then Comes Silence, and A Projection. The Sun Came Up Tremendously follows the band’s 2024 album Our Ashes at the End of the Day. Its ten songs were written between 2024 and 2025, then recorded and produced at Thommy Hein Studios in Berlin from late 2025 into early 2026. Resistance was mixed by Thommy Hein and Peer Lebrecht and mastered by Hein, who also contributes guest guitar. The current Golden Apes lineup comprises Peer Lebrecht on vocals and synths, Maximilian Hennig and Stephan Schönefeld on guitars, Christian Lebrecht on bass, and Salomon Bosse on drums. “…o sun, that healest all distempered vision, thou dost content me so, when thou resolvest, that doubting pleases me no less than knowing!” – Dante Alighieri, Divina Commedia Listen to Resistance below, and pre-order The Sun Came Up Tremendously through Bandcamp. The album arrives September 18 via Icy Cold Records.
